title: DSM-108 Full Course Recap
kicker: DSM-108 Spreadsheet Modeling · full course recap · S1–S10 (Ray Sanjog)

footer: Full-course recap for DSM-108 Spreadsheet Modeling, S1–S10 (Ray Sanjog). Built from the lecture notes in lectures/. The SIP, EMI, Goal Seek and break-even figures were recomputed from the stated formulas (annuity-due FV, PMT, FC/(P−VC)) and match the lecture values. Cell addresses, and the bonus-slab table in module 6, are reconstructions from ASR transcripts and are flagged where they appear. The widgets replay the lecture's own examples: the ₹20,000 SIP, the 9×9 multiplication table, the second-highest-quarter quiz problem, the bonus slab table, the ₹20 lakh loan model and the bike break-even problem.
course_notes: Central contrast, repeated in almost every session: amber = the static answer (a typed or hard-coded number, manual colouring, 'select → insert', a formula that returns only the first match); teal = the live, formula-driven model (named cells, $/mixed references, the function that fits the scenario, outputs that recompute when inputs or data change). The instructor's refrains are 'never hard-code', 'the real skill is knowing which function is most appropriate' and 'if the model is wrong, all these values will be wrong'. Instructor: Ray Sanjog; write only faculty names, never students. Units: rupees in Indian notation (lakh/crore; 1 crore = 100 lakh) for the SIP, loan, bike and player-salary examples; the sales dataset uses a 'Dollars' field, but its total was spoken as '2,39,000 / ₹2.39 lakh', so label it 'Dollars (field)' without a currency claim. Exam statements in the notes: Quiz (S4): hands-on in Excel, not MCQ, 30 min, 40% weight, covers S1–6. S7 says the quiz covers up to S7 and runs 30–45 min. The S10 review shows the quiz was 50 marks (22+22+6) with step-wise partial credit. End-term (S10): 1 hour, most likely 3 questions. S8 states '45 minutes, one dataset, three questions', so show both and flag the difference. The end-term is guaranteed one question on Developer-tab form controls and formula-based conditional formatting, and one on What-If analysis (S9, S10). Pivot dashboards are a major focus; a subjective dashboard question is possible (S4, S5). Chart titles must match the question exactly (S5). Data tables must show {=TABLE()} braces (S8). If a question says 'use VLOOKUP only', any other function scores zero (S10). Submit the Excel file through the platform/office, with email as fallback. Grading is relative (S9). No ChatGPT or AI in the exam (S10). Reference book: Excel Bible. Solver was installed but NOT covered.

modules.plan: Module 'Formula hygiene, named cells and the SIP' (S1). Content type: numerical. Cheat cards: (1) the four good-practice rules that carry marks: never type ₹/$ by hand, because the cell becomes text and arithmetic fails; enter rates as 13%, with no /100 inside formulas; no hard-coded literals like =20000*13/100; no spaces in names, since Create from Selection turns spaces into _. (2) Named cells, two ways: the Name Box for one cell, or Formulas → Create from Selection → Left column for many. Check them in Name Manager; audit with Formulas → Show Formulas. (3) SI = P·r·t; CI = P(1+r)^t − P; the ^ operator vs POWER(number, power). (4) The fx dialog: argument help appears only after the opening bracket; bold arguments are required. (5) FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type]) as an argument table: rate per period = 13%/12 (/4 quarterly); type 1 = beginning of period, 0 or omitted = end; sign convention (cash out is negative, so put a minus on pmt or on FV). FV applies only if payment, rate and periodicity are all constant. (6) Manual SIP: each deposit is an independent investment with tenure 12, 11, …, 1. Columns: Month (fill handle), SIP, monthly rate =$B$3/12, tenure, value =B6*(1+C6)^D6, % contribution =E6/$E$18. (7) Absolute reference: F4 cycles $B$3 → B$3 → $B3 → B3. (8) Large-data habits: click A1 first, then Data → Get Data → From Text/CSV → Load; Table Design → Convert to Range; navigation shortcut table (Ctrl+↓, Ctrl+Shift+↓, Ctrl+Home, Ctrl+End); filter first (Ctrl+Shift+L); Freeze Top Row (edges only, never a middle block); name a whole column via Ctrl+Shift+↓ + Name Box; COUNT counts numbers only (COUNTA for text IDs); =SUM(Total_Price). Notes/analogies: 'fx is your guide', since exams may contain functions you have never seen (S1). Named cells are like well-named variables in code: you, or whoever you email, reopen =B1*B3*B2 weeks later and cannot read it. Named cells earn marks in the exam (S1; repeated S2, and in the S10 recap '=Revenue*Margin instead of =B1*B5*B27'). 'Don't just trust Excel. Understand what it does behind the scenes', which is why the SIP is also done by hand (S1). FV breaks as soon as the SIP grows (e.g. 10% a year) or the rate changes; then only the 'independent deposits' logic works (S1). A ₹ typed by hand silently turns a number into text (S1). ONE widget, 'SIP ledger', replays the S1 problem: ₹20,000 on the 1st of every month at 13% p.a., valued on 31 Dec. Twelve rows Jan–Dec show tenure (months), value 20000·(1+i)^n, and % contribution as a thin bar. A timing toggle switches between type = 1 (deposit on the 1st, tenures 12…1) and type = 0 (end of month, tenures 11…0). Readouts: the manual SUM, the equivalent formula text =-FV(13%/12,12,20000,0,1) or the type-0 version, and its value. Verdict is teal for type 1 ('₹2,57,589.85: matches FV with type = 1') and amber for type 0 ('≈ ₹2,54,829: you modelled end-of-month deposits, wrong here'). An optional rate slider (6–20%, default 13%) shows that the manual sum and FV agree at every rate. Worked problems: SI on ₹20,000 at 13% for 1 year (₹2,600, equal to CI when t = 1); the SIP solved by FV and by hand; count the orders and total the prices with named columns.
modules.facts: SI: 20,000 × 0.13 × 1 = 2,600 (SI = CI when t = 1). Time ambiguity (transcript also says 'to the power 10'): with t = 10, A = 20,000 × 1.13^10 ≈ 67,891 and CI ≈ 47,891. A student's '27,800' is unexplained; flag it, don't show it. SIP: i = 0.13/12 = 0.0108333; (1+i)^12 ≈ 1.138032; FV due = 20,000 × ((1+i)^12 − 1)/i × (1+i) ≈ 257,589 (lecture: ₹2,57,589.85). End-of-month (type 0) = 20,000 × ((1+i)^12 − 1)/i ≈ 254,828 (notes: ₹2,54,829). Per-row values (computed, not read in class): Jan = 20,000 × 1.138032 ≈ 22,760.6; Dec = 20,000 × 1.0108333 ≈ 20,216.7; % contribution Jan ≈ 22,760.6/257,589 ≈ 8.84%, Dec ≈ 7.85%. ASR 'divided by 0.183' = 'divided by 12'. FV formula string: =FV(13%/12, 12, -20000, 0, 1).

modules.plan: Module 'Choosing and building the right chart' (S1–S3). Content type: framework / case (decision tables). ZERO widgets: the notes give no per-state, monthly or heat-map grid values, so any chart would be invented. Cheat cards as a decision table 'question → chart → data layout Excel needs': parent/child, 'biggest parent AND biggest brand' → Treemap or Sunburst (or a decomposition tree), with columns in Parent | Child | Value order, Banner labels, and Value data labels. Only one category has children → Pie of Pie: Split by Position counts from the BOTTOM, so cut the child rows to the bottom and set 'values in second plot = 3'; rename 'Other' to the parent; tick Percentage, untick Value. Several brands with children → back to the treemap. Actual vs forecast → line chart with the forecast in its own column ('Forecasted Sales'), the junction value 34,000 copied into both columns, and Dash type dotted. Target vs actual → bullet chart built as a combo: Target as a wide primary bar (low gap width), Actual as a thin bar on the secondary axis (high gap width); set the secondary max from 4.5 to 5, then delete it. The S3 variant adds an Average column changed to Scatter, with markers forming the line. Many trends on one page → Sparklines (Line/Column/Win-Loss; the location range has one cell per data row; Win/Loss needs a +1/0/−1 helper =IF(C2>B2,1,IF(C2<B2,-1,0)), or SIGN). Day × hour intensity → Color Scales heat map: format the totals blocks separately, hide numbers with ;;; (sections positive;negative;zero;text), and build the legend from a 1…6 row with the same scale. In-cell indicators: nested IF status (+1/−1/0, don't forget the equal case) with a 3-icon set and Show Icon Only (default thresholds 67%/33% of range; Manage Rules → This Worksheet); arrows via absolute refs to symbol cells; REPT('|', Sales/10000), which drops decimals. Missing value: =NA() or blank, plus Select Data → Hidden and Empty Cells → Connect data points and 'Show #N/A as empty'; never 0. Protection: Format Cells → Protection → Hidden AND Review → Protect Sheet (both needed); file password via Save As → Tools → General Options. Notes/analogies: 'Select → Insert will never work on my questions' (S2). 'Number of columns = number of colours' (S2, repeated S3; S10 recap). The S10 quiz Q1 colour chart was won or lost on the IF helper table, so add a one-line cross-reference. 'If you have to study the chart, it's a bad chart': a basic chart pointed at Rajasthan, the bullet chart shows West Bengal (S2). A Pie of Pie that looks the same but has different numbers is a different chart (S2). Connecting the missing October point invents a slope nobody measured; 0 fakes a crash (S2). Moving axis bounds can make a small change look dramatic (S2). Smoothed lines look nice but are 'not a right idea' analytically (S2). Mismatched dual axes (5 vs 4.5) made actuals look below target: 'two axes must share the same scale' (S2, S3). Don't mix rectangles in a heat map, and don't colour by hand (S3). Sparklines are the tiny stock-trend lines in newspapers; Win/Loss is the intraday-trading green/red strip (S3). Show a static layout table (Month | Sales 2016 | Forecasted Sales 2017 with the 34,000 junction row in both columns) and a 'rules to memorise' card. Worked problems: smartphone treemap (BBK Electronics biggest parent via Vivo/Realme/Oppo; Xiaomi biggest single brand); bullet-chart reading against target and against the average; heat-map reading.

modules.plan: Module 'Referencing, statistical, random and choice functions' (S3–S4). Content type: algorithmic. Cheat cards: (1) Reference types: absolute $B$2, relative B2, and mixed $A2 / B$1. The one-formula 9×9 multiplication table: headers 1–9 in A2:A10 and, via Paste Special → Transpose, B1:J1; =$A2*B$1 in B2, dragged right and down. (2) Circular reference: discount =IF(Profit>0, SP×Disc%, 0) and Profit = SP − CP − Discount. 'If you get the pop-up you built it correctly'. Enable via File → Options → Formulas → Enable iterative calculation (Mac: Preferences → Calculation). Auditing tools: Trace Precedents/Dependents, Remove Arrows, Evaluate Formula. (3) Statistics on a named range 'marks': MAX, MIN, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE.SNGL, LARGE(marks,k), SMALL(marks,k). RANK.EQ(x, marks, 0), where 0/omitted = descending. (4) The union-reference trick for ranking a value nobody scored: =RANK.EQ(D10,(marks,D10),0). (5) Random/sequence functions: RANDBETWEEN(1,36); RANDARRAY(rows, cols, min, max, whole); RAND() in [0,1); SEQUENCE(rows, cols, start, step). Spill: the formula lives only in the top-left cell. F9 recalculates. Volatile functions should be frozen with Paste Special → Values. (6) Unique random 1–10: RAND() then RANK.EQ (instructor), or =SORTBY(SEQUENCE(10),RANDARRAY(10)) (class solution). ROUND(RAND()*10,0) can repeat and can give 0. (7) CHOOSE(index, v1, …) replaces long nested IFs for a fixed indexed list, e.g. random group A–F =CHOOSE(RANDBETWEEN-frozen,'A',…,'F'). (8) Weekday name: WEEKDAY (Sunday = 1) + CHOOSE, or TEXT(date,'dddd'); TODAY()+5. (9) ROW(), COLUMN(); array constants use commas {1,2,3}. Notes/analogies: 'This is like exam where many people get zero, complete zero': answering #N/A for a score of 28, which is a valid mark on 0–50 and so must have a rank (S3). Circular references are 'for knowledge only'. Add the notes' caveat that the CP = 110 case oscillates: discount 12 makes profit −2, so no discount, so profit 10, so the discount applies again (S3). 'Solve it with logic, not Google' for the unique-numbers puzzle; RANDARRAY in class gave 10 three times and 7 twice (S3). The instructor admitted he couldn't follow the one-line SORTBY answer but agreed it was right; explain why it works (S3). Using nested IF where CHOOSE fits still earns credit but may cost about 1 mark: 'knowing when to use which function is the real skill' (S4). Live RANDBETWEEN keeps changing your groups; freeze it (S4). TWO widgets. (a) 'Drag the formula': the 9×9 table with a mode switch between =A2*B1 (relative), =$A$2*$B$1 (absolute) and =$A2*B$1 (mixed). Clicking any cell shows the rewritten formula in a fake formula bar and highlights the two cells it points at: teal if a header, amber if inside the table. Values are computed for real: relative mode gives chained products (row 2 becomes 1, 2, 6, 24 …), absolute gives 1 everywhere, mixed gives the times table. The verdict names the only correct mode. (b) 'Unique random numbers for 10 people': a 'Recalculate (F9)' button redraws two columns, RANDBETWEEN(1,10) with duplicates outlined amber plus a duplicate count, and RAND() + RANK.EQ showing a teal permutation of 1–10 every time. Caption: ties of RAND() are possible but negligible. Worked problems: rank of 31 (14) and of 28 via the union reference; circular discount with CP 100 vs 110; weekday of 18 Sep 2026 via CHOOSE(WEEKDAY()).
modules.facts: Mixed formula =$A2*B$1, so cell (i, j) = row header i × column header j. Relative chain (computed): B2 = A2·B1 = 1·1 = 1; C2 = B2·C1 = 1·2 = 2; D2 = C2·D1 = 2·3 = 6; E2 = 6·4 = 24; B3 = A3·B2 = 2·1 = 2. Absolute: every cell = A2·B1 = 1. Discount model (CP 100, SP 120, 10%): discount 120 × 0.10 = 12; profit 120 − 100 − 12 = 8. CP 110: lecture reading 'no discount', profit 120 − 110 = 10; with the discount, 120 − 110 − 12 = −2 (oscillation caveat added by the notes). RANK.EQ(31, marks, 0) = 14; RANK.EQ(28, …) = #N/A (nobody scored 28). Marks range 0–50. RANDBETWEEN(1,36) showed 31 (transcript also says 30). RANDARRAY(10,1,1,10,TRUE) in class: 10 appeared 3 times, 7 twice. SEQUENCE(20,1,0,5) → 0, 5, 10, 15, … (ASR '0 5 15 25' is wrong). RAND × 10 example: 0.87379 × 10 = 8.7379. WEEKDAY(18 Sep 2026) = 6 (Friday, Sunday = 1); 16 Sep 2026 = Wednesday. Random groups: RANDBETWEEN(1,6) → CHOOSE to A–F. S4's '+ three' WEEKDAY offset is unclear (ASR); no offset is needed with the default numbering.

modules.plan: Module 'Pivot tables and the interactive dashboard' (S4–S5). Content type: framework / procedural. ZERO widgets: the content is checklists and connection rules, and the notes give no transaction-level data. Cheat cards: (1) Pivot habits: start with a question; Insert → PivotTable → From Table/Range; name every pivot (PivotTable Analyze → PivotTable Name); drag fields rather than ticking them; Design → Grand Totals → Off. Value Field Settings: Sum/Average/Count/Max/Min, with text fields defaulting to Count. Show Values As → % of Grand Total. Copy-paste a pivot to make the next one. Restore the Field List via PivotTable Analyze → Field List. Empty-cell display in PivotTable Options. (2) Top-20% highlight: select only the numeric cells, then Conditional Formatting → Top/Bottom → Top 10% with 10 changed to 20. Value Filters → Top 10. Sort by value via More Sort Options → by Sum of …, not by label. (3) Pivot chart vs normal chart: a pivot chart has field filter buttons (hide them on dashboards). (4) Grouping: right-click → Group → By. (5) Count a unique ID (Transaction Number), never Name. (6) GETPIVOTDATA: type = and click the pivot cell, never type the value. SUMIFS is an acceptable alternative. (7) Calculated field: Fields, Items & Sets → Calculated Field → Price per Unit = Dollars/Units, which equals ΣDollars/ΣUnits, a weighted average. (8) Slicers (Ctrl-click for several) and Timelines (date fields only; Years/Quarters/Months/Days). (9) The dashboard recipe as a numbered checklist: PTAll (Total Sales) → slicer on Name from PTAll → PTSelect → % Selected = Selected/Total → PTPie doughnut (title 'Product Sales', hide field buttons) → PTHeat (Product × Months; Move PivotTable onto the dashboard; colour scale; ;;; ; column width 5) → PTBar (calculated field, 4 decimals, data labels, no fill/outline) → PTSpark (Years + Quarters expanded, no subtotals; select the destination cell FIRST, then Insert → Sparklines → Line) → Timeline from the first pivot → Report Connections for slicer AND timeline: check everything except PTAll. Remove gridlines. (10) A Report Connections table with rows = the 6 pivots and columns = Slicer / Timeline (✓ for all but PTAll), plus the rule 'any checked pivot moves when you click'. (11) No overlapping pivots: clear all filters before placing a new one; an error while copying usually means overlap. Notes/analogies: 'Start with a question in mind', storyboard first; don't dump everything into a pivot (S4). 'Name every pivot' is 'very critical', because unnamed pivots show up as 'PivotTable86' in Report Connections (S4, S5). 'Remove the grand total, it doesn't look nice' (S4). Two salespeople can share a name, so count the transaction number (S4). Average of Units is the average quantity, not the price (S4). The level of aggregation changes the answer: the same data crowns age 50 (F) or 44/46 (M), then 25–34, then 55–59 depending on the bin (S4). The class first pasted the travel data into the dashboard file and got 8409, the wrong total (S4). One pivot per question beats one cluttered pivot (S4). At 2 decimals the price bars look identical (all ≈ 3.05); switch to 4 (S5). Forgetting to connect a new pivot, or to uncheck PTAll on the timeline, is the common mistake (S5). The critique: 'not a very good dashboard', because 'who is the best salesperson?' needs a click per name; 'pivot table is not always the best idea', which leads into module 5 (S5). Exam lines: chart titles must match the question exactly, and a dashboard-building question is expected (S4, S5). Show a static grouping table (individual / 10 / 5 / 3 years → top group). Worked problems: count transactions (1891); Jen's lipstick sales via GETPIVOTDATA; price per unit as a calculated field; % of total for one selected salesperson.
modules.facts: Travel data: 925 people; gender difference negligible (male average slightly higher). Top-20% ages: 25, 27, 39, 44, 46, 55. Individual-age top spenders: 50 (female); 44 and 46 (male); older females and younger males spend most. Grouping: by 10 → 25–34; by 5 → 55–59 (male), 44 no longer stands out; by 3 → different again. Sales data: 1891 transactions; 5 products (incl. Lipstick, Foundation, Eyeliner). Total sales ≈ 2,39,000 (spoken as ₹2.39 lakh; the field is 'Dollars'). Wrong total from pasting the travel data: 8409. One salesperson selected ≈ 10% of total (dollar figure garbled: '10.37 224'). Price per unit ≈ 3.05 for all products, shown to 4 decimals. Heat-map column width 5. Timeline demo: April at month level. Pivot names: S4 used PTTotal/PTSelected, S5 PTAll/PTSelect/PTPie/PTHeat/PTBar/PTSpark (use the S5 set). GETPIVOTDATA example: =GETPIVOTDATA("Dollars",$A$3,"Name","Jen","Product","Lipstick") (anchor inferred).

modules.plan: Module 'Conditional aggregation and array retrieval' (S5–S6). Content type: algorithmic + code. Cheat cards: (1) SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range); SUMIFS(sum_range FIRST, then range/criteria pairs in any order); COUNTIF/COUNTIFS. Named ranges Dollars/Units/Name; the unique list via Data → Remove Duplicates. (2) Criteria against a cell: COUNTIF(Units, ">"&L10). Writing ">L10" returns 0 because it is literal text. & concatenates ('xx'&'yy' = 'xxyy'). (3) All ranges in SUMIFS/COUNTIFS must be the same size, or you get #VALUE!. (4) MATCH(value, array, 0), where 0 = exact and is 'very critical'; INDEX(array, row, [col]); nested INDEX(Name, MATCH(G2, Salary, 0)). INDEX(whole block, MATCH(…), {1,3}) spills two columns. Named ranges must start on the same row. (5) The family table: arrays → MATCH/INDEX/XMATCH/XLOOKUP; tables → VLOOKUP/HLOOKUP. First-occurrence functions (MATCH, INDEX, XLOOKUP, VLOOKUP, LOOKUP) vs array functions (FILTER, SORT). (6) The retrieval screen: Data Validation → List drop-down; =FILTER(Name, Country=G9); =FILTER(HSTACK(Name, Salary), Country=G9); SORT(…, 2, −1); the robust top earner =FILTER(Name, (Country=G9)*(Salary=MAXIFS(Salary, Country, G9))), where * = AND. Spilled cells show a greyed formula. (7) Second-highest quarter → group: LARGE(row,2) → MATCH(…,0) → INDEX($B$2:$E$2, pos), or the one-liner. Ties go to the earlier quarter because MATCH scans left to right. (8) Latest quarter on ties: XMATCH(v, row, 0, −1), or XLOOKUP(LARGE(row,2), row, headers, , 0, −1); search_mode −1 = last to first. Notes/analogies: the COUNTIF above-average question is 'the trick question' set on past exams; a hard-coded average is not accepted even if the number is right (S5). A student's F:F column references produced #VALUE! (S5). 'Occam's razor': SORT first, then the tie test. Make Buttler's salary equal England's top and the 'first row' answer silently drops a name (S6). 'Your exam question will be exactly like this. Some screen will be given. You have to design that' (S6). 'Always break into smaller parts': value → position → label; 'it doesn't take even one minute to solve' (S6). Nested IFs are 'not a technique'; the old LOOKUP is 'very complicated… not very popular' (S6). Rule: test every formula against a tie; returning only the first of several answers is marked wrong (S6). Forgetting the 0 in MATCH is the frequent error (S6). ONE widget, 'Second-highest quarter stepper' (Player with .viz-body, pre.pcode, .vars). The stage shows a row Q1–Q4 with group labels A–D above. Preset 1 is the lecture's tie row: Q2 = 318 and Q3 = 318; the other quarters are shown as 'other value (not in notes)', with a note that neither equals 318. Steps: (1) v = LARGE(row,2) = 318, pcode line 1 highlighted. (2) MATCH(v,row,0) scans left to right: Q1 grey 'no', Q2 teal 'hit', pos = 2. (3) INDEX(headers, 2) = B, the earlier-quarter rule. (4) The rule switches to 'latest quarter': XMATCH(v,row,0,−1) scans right to left, Q4 'no', Q3 hit, pos = 3, with the arrow direction animated. (5) INDEX → C. Vars panel: v, scan direction, pos, label. Preset 2 is the first employee row: v = 541 found at Q1 → A. A closing card gives the XLOOKUP one-liner. Worked problems: COUNTIF above average (917); Betsy's sales with Units > 1 via SUMIFS; the player retrieval screen with the tie test.

modules.plan: Module 'Designing lookup tables: VLOOKUP, HLOOKUP, XLOOKUP, SUMPRODUCT' (S7, plus the S10 quiz Q2 review). Content type: algorithmic + code. Cheat cards: (1) The four VLOOKUP/HLOOKUP assumptions: a lookup table exists (you usually build it); the key is in the leftmost column / top row; approximate match needs an ASCENDING sort; the column/row index counts from the key column. (2) Syntax and range_lookup: FALSE = exact, TRUE/omitted = largest key ≤ value. Use FALSE for text keys such as T1 or P1. (3) Named range (V_Bonus, H_Bonus) vs $-locked range when dragging. Build the horizontal copy with Paste Special → Transpose. (4) Below the first slab: add a 0 → 0 row rather than an IF; IFERROR is the alternative. (5) SUMPRODUCT(a, b, …) = Σ aᵢbᵢ over equal-sized arrays; F4 on the fixed multiplier row. (6) VLOOKUP(A2, Product, {2,3,4}, FALSE) spills price, threshold and discount%. Then the helper columns: Discount applied =IF(Qty>=Threshold, Disc%, 0); Amount before = Qty × Price; Discount amount = before × applied; Paid = before − discount. (7) Two tables: robust =IF(C2<3, VLOOKUP(B2,LT3,2,TRUE), VLOOKUP(B2,GT3,2,TRUE)) vs compact =VLOOKUP(B2, IF(C2<3,LT3,GT3), 2), which assumes the same return column. (8) XLOOKUP(value, lookup, return, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]), match_mode: 0 exact, −1 next smaller, 1 next larger, 2 wildcard. The upper-slab formula =IFERROR(XLOOKUP(B2,$H$4:$H$9,$I$4:$I$9,,1), MAX($I$4:$I$9)). (9) S10 quiz Q2 pattern: RANK.EQ computed, never typed, plus a VLOOKUP cut-off table whose rank boundaries are driven by an input % (e.g. =ROUNDUP($H$1*COUNT(range),0)+1) with approximate match; 'only VLOOKUP allowed, other functions scored zero'. Notes/analogies: the telephone directory: give a number, get the name (S7). 'Nobody hands you the table': designing it is the real skill (S7). The 500 challenge: fix it without an IF and without touching the formula, by adding a 0 row (S7). FALSE for text keys: TRUE 'might happen to give the right answer' but is technically wrong, flagged repeatedly (S7). 'Don't fix your mind on one formula; know each function's restrictions' (S7, upper-slab problem). 300 typed into if_not_found was rejected as hard-coding; MAX of the bonus column replaces it (S7). IFERROR must go in the first cell before dragging (S7). Robust vs compact: choose robustness when the tables could differ (S7). The instructor's slip 'sorted and descending' is wrong; ascending is right (S7). The real hard part of the quiz was the dynamic cut-off table (S10). ONE widget, 'Slab lookup lab', with a banner: 'slab table reconstructed from the lecture's answers; the 3,000 row is inferred'. Table rows 1,000→50, 2,000→100, 3,000→200, 5,000→300, with a toggle 'add 0 → 0 row'. Sales slider 0–8,000 with lecture presets 500, 2,000, 2,700, 4,300, 7,000, 7,611. Three readout rows: VLOOKUP(…,TRUE) highlights the matched row from below (next smaller); XLOOKUP(…,1) highlights from above (next larger); IFERROR(XLOOKUP, MAX). #N/A cells are shown amber. Verdict lines: '500 without the 0 row → #N/A; with it → 0'; '2,700: VLOOKUP gives the lower slab 100, the upper-slab rule needs XLOOKUP → 200'; '7,611: XLOOKUP finds no larger key → IFERROR returns MAX = 300'. Worked problems: weighted hours by SUMPRODUCT (32.25); the product-discount helper columns; the upper-slab bonus for 2,700 and 4,300.

modules.plan: Module 'What-If analysis: data tables, Goal Seek, Scenario Manager' (S8). Content type: numerical. One line: a What-If question is guaranteed in the end-term. Cheat cards: (1) The loan model: inputs Loan (B1), Rate (B2), Tenure (B3); outputs EMI =-PMT(B2/12, B3*12, B1) in B6, Total = EMI × tenure × 12 in B7, Extra = Total − Loan in B8. Name cells with Create from Selection. (2) PMT(rate, nper, pv, [fv], [type]): rate per period, nper = years × 12, fv = 0 to pay off fully, type 0 = end (default) / 1 = beginning. Constant rate and payment only. EMI = P·r·(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n − 1). (3) One-way data table: inputs down the LEFT column; the formula row sits one row up and one column right (several outputs allowed); select without headings; Column input cell = the varied input; result {=TABLE(,B3)}. (4) Two-way: rates down the left, tenures across the top (Transpose), ONE output in the corner cell; Row input = top-row variable, Column input = left-column variable; {=TABLE(B3,B2)}; optional colour scale. One-way vs two-way comparison table. (5) Data tables are live: they recalculate on any non-varied input change; Paste Values to freeze. (6) Goal Seek: Set cell / To value / By changing exactly one input; works backwards. (7) Scenario Manager: Add → changing cells B1:B3 → values; Summary vs Scenario PivotTable report; result cells B6, B8. It is a reporting tool and does no optimisation. (8) Break-even: Profit = P·Q − (FC + VC·Q); Q* = FC/(P − VC). (9) How the instructor grades: model first (he changes an input), then the {=TABLE()} braces, then Scenario values he specified; Goal Seek is the intended method. (10) OFFSET dynamic chart: show, labelled NOT examinable. Notes/analogies: 'Pay your loan off as early as possible': at 20 years the extra exceeds the loan (S8). Forgetting /12 live gave an EMI of several lakh a month (S8). 'If the model is wrong, all these values will be wrong'; 'if the model is right, all of them will be right' (S8). Typed-and-dragged formulas have no braces and don't count as a data table (S8). The instructor expected about 40 lakh for a ₹50,000 EMI, but EMI is linear in the loan: ×1.89 → 37.8 lakh (S8). Naming pays off when the Scenario report shows Loan_amount instead of $B$1 (S8). Harder twist to expect: bikes produced ≠ bikes sold (S8). Reset inputs after Goal Seek (price back to 2,100, tenure back to 10) (S8). TWO widgets. (a) 'Loan model and its tables': sliders for loan (₹10–40 L, default 20 L), rate (6–20%, default 10%) and tenure (5–25 yrs, default 10), plus a type toggle 0/1. Readouts: EMI, Total, Extra, and a teal/amber verdict 'extra paid exceeds the loan' when it does. Below sit the one-way tenure table (8, 10, 12, 15, 18, 20), the one-way rate table (8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 20%) and the two-way EMI grid with a colour scale. The cell matching the current inputs is outlined. A small 'reacts to' tag shows which tables change for each slider: the tenure table ignores the tenure slider, the rate table doesn't. Buttons: Goal Seek 'EMI = 50,000 by changing tenure' (→ 4.07 yrs) and 'by changing loan' (tenure reset to 10 → ₹37.8 L). Scenario presets Best / Worst / Base fill the sliders and a mini Scenario Summary table (EMI, Extra). (b) 'Bike break-even': FC 4,45,000 and VC 1,100 fixed; a price slider (1,200–2,500, presets 2,100 and 1,800) and a bikes slider (0–1,000, default 100). Chart of Revenue and Expenses lines over 0–1,000 with the crossing marked. Readouts: Revenue, Expenses, Profit, Q* = FC/(P − VC) rounded up. The 200–700 one-way table recomputes. Verdict: loss/profit at the chosen volume. Worked problems: EMI and extra for 10 vs 20 years; Goal Seek for tenure and for loan; bike Q1–Q4 (table, 445, 636, two-way checks).

Module 'Form controls, formula-based conditional formatting, macros and the Analysis ToolPak' (S9–S10). Content type: framework / procedural with code snippets. ZERO widgets: the notes contain no grid digits, chart series, stock prices, MPG rows or marks, so nothing can be replayed with lecture numbers. One line: a question on form controls + CF is guaranteed in the end-term. Cheat cards: (1) Enable Developer via File → Options → Customize Ribbon → tick Developer; Developer → Excel Add-ins → Analysis ToolPak + Solver Add-in. Use Form Controls, never ActiveX. (2) Checkbox cell link: right-click → Format Control → Control → Cell link, giving TRUE/FALSE ('I will definitely give some question on this'). (3) CF with a formula: select the grid with the first cell active, then New Rule → Use a formula. Keep the grid ref relative and the link absolute: =AND(G11=0,$Z$1); '2 or 3' =AND(OR(G11=2,G11=3),$Z$3); in-cell Insert → Checkbox, where the cell itself holds TRUE/FALSE, so =A2 (or =$A2 for the adjacent column). (4) Show/hide a chart series: flag =IF(link,1,NA()), helper = value × $flag; #N/A points aren't drawn, while 0 draws a flat line. (5) Ratio dashboard: net margin = NPAT/Sales, asset turnover = Sales/Total assets, equity multiplier = Total assets/Equity, ROE = NPAT/Equity (DuPont product). Status =IF($H$2, IF(AND(F4>E4,F4>D4),'Better', IF(AND(F4<E4,F4<D4),'Worse','Average')), '') with the third label inferred. Highlight Cells Rules for every possible label. (6) The combo box returns a POSITION (1–4), not a name, so use =INDEX($A$4:$G$7,$J$2,col), optionally wrapped in IFERROR. (7) Macros: Record Macro → act → Stop; Developer → Macros → Edit to change 'Worse' to 'Bad' in VBA (Sub … End Sub); Insert → Form Controls → Button → Assign Macro; navigation macros RTA / RA between sheets; save as .xlsm, because .xlsx drops macros. Show the reconstructed VBA as a code card marked inferred. (8) ToolPak: Descriptive Statistics (Input incl. headers, Labels in first row, Summary statistics must be ticked), with STDEV.S because a time window is a sample. Correlation, where the diagonal 1s defeat MAX, so highlight with =B2=LARGE(matrix, ROWS(matrix)+1). Regression: Input Y = mpg, X = 5 predictors, Labels, read P-values < 0.05. Histogram: marks without the header, Bin Range 0, 5, …, 50, no Pareto, Chart Output; manual COUNTIFS or FREQUENCY. (9) Exam-rule card from the S10 quiz review: step-wise marks, helper tables carry the weight, never hard-code ranks or cut-offs, highlights must be formula-based, Q3 Value Filters → Top 10 → Top 1 was all-or-nothing. Notes/analogies: 'Record Macro works like a phone camera': everything between Record and Stop is replayed (S10). 'Please be clear on that': Form Controls only (S9). Excel silently wrapped a CF formula in double quotes; fix it in Manage Rules (S9). "NA" is just the letters N-A; NA() is a function (S9). 'There are multiple ways… but the best thing is the NA thing', which is the same trick as the quiz's positive/negative colour question (S9). Add the 'Better' rule even if no row shows it today, because the data may change (S9). Don't click another tab mid-formula or the reference 'goes away' (S9). The ToolPak is the free substitute for SPSS/SAS (S10). Several students highlighted two cells or did it by hand; 'there is only one answer' (S10). Sorting the marks and plotting them can't show a bell (S10). The office checks the first page of every grade sheet for a bell-shaped histogram (S10). Bins of width 1 gave mostly zeros; width 5 shows the shape (S10). The skew note: mass at the high end with a tail to low marks is NEGATIVE skew, although it was called 'positive' in class (S10). 'The real skill is knowing which function is most appropriate for a given problem' (S10 recap). Don't use ChatGPT in the exam; students have been caught (S10). Worked problems: the '2 or 3' orange rule; the status column hidden behind a checkbox; the correlation highlight (Intel–Microsoft); the regression verdict (HP and Weight significant).
